newsitem.title: USA: Olympic bomb suspect sets up aid hotline.
newsitem.headline: Olympic bomb suspect sets up aid hotline.

text.p: Olympic Games bomb suspect Richard Jewell has set up a telephone hotline to take financial contributions from the public to help him clear his name, his lawyers on Tuesday.
The Richard Jewell Fund was created to provide support for the unemployed security guard and his mother, Barbara, while also helping to meet the growing bills from his four-member legal team.

A statement announcing the fund said Jewell's life had been turned into a "nightmare" by the bomb case. It called him "an innocent man ... being held hostage by the FBI and the media without any evidence to charge him with a crime."
Jewell, 33, is the only named suspect in the federal investigation into the July 27 bombing at Atlanta's Centennial Olympic Park, which left two dead and more than 100 injured.
He was working as a security guard at an Olympic Park pavilion operated by sponsor AT&T Corp.

Jewell was hailed initially as a hero for finding the pipe bomb before it went off. But soon afterwards, he was identified as a suspect and has lived ever since as a near recluse because of FBI and media surveillance.
While he remained under the watch of federal investigators on Monday, an FBI spokesman declined to comment on the case.
On Sunday, Jewell told CBS' 60 Minutes that he and his lawyers planned to sue everyone who had libelled him.

"I hate even asking for money but the fact is we're going to be engaged in a long, expensive process. A lot of people have offered to help and we'd just like to take advantage of those offers," said Jewell's chief attorney, G. Watson Bryant.

"Richard can't work and he's got his truck payments and various other odds and ends that he needs some help to get by on. And his mom? She is on a shoe-string budget, but she can't have the extra mouths to feed without some help."
Bryant said he had received unsolicited financial contributions from the public for about two months, though the total had not approached $1,000.
State officials have taken action against the security agency which employed Jewell, saying they never had a license to operate in Georgia.
Anthony Davis Associates of Los Angeles was hired by AT&T Corp to provide security at its Olympic pavilion.

A spokeswoman for Georgia Secretary of State Lewis Massey said Georgia officials had turned evidence of a misdemeanor charge over to local prosecutors and asked the agency to stop operating within state boundaries.
Officials with the Los Angeles-based agency were not immediately available for comment.
